Vigilance Set Up in ISRO 
5. The Indian Space Research Organisation is the space agency of Government of India 
and has its headquarters in Bengaluru . The Committee visited Bengaluru during its study 
visit to Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Mumbai from 14 th to 18 th January, 2020 to ma ke an 
appraisal of the vigilance administration of several PSUs and PSBs. 
5.1 ISRO was established in 1969 . It comes under  the Department of Space, which 
reports to the Prime Minister of India. ISRO has a part time CVO. The Chief Vigilance 
Officer, Department of Space heads its Vigilance Division, however, the Joint Secretary 
(Administration) of the Department is designated as part time Chief Vigilance Officer of 
ISRO and is responsible for the overall vigilance administration of the Department. Ever y 
ISRO Centre/Unit has a Vigilance Wing headed by Vigilance Officer who reports to CVO. 
5.2 With regard to preventive vigilance, Joint Secretary (Administration ) informed the 
Committee that all p rocurement in ISRO is done through respective Committees and there 
are different Committees to deal with tenders of different values. Surprise inspections are 
conducted at ISRO Centres/Units by the vigilance officials. Intelligence inputs on security 
and vigilance matters are collected from CISF and utilized as inpu ts to strengthen vigilance. 
The Department implements rotation transfer policy in certain administrative areas which are 
vulnerable to corruption. Rotation of S&T personnel posted in different technical domains at 
ISRO Centres/Units is not always feasible.  The Committee has been apprised that ISRO is 
exploring the feasibility of implementing integrity pact in various types of procurement 
contracts as the Department’s procurement mostly consists of sophisticated technical items. 
5.3 On the issue of punitive vigilance, she informed that a Group ‘A’ officer of 
Semiconductor Laboratory, Chandigarh was imposed minor penalty of censure for 
procedural irregularity in 2016 in processing of contract after due consultation with CVC and 
three s anctions for prosecution were issued in 2017 by the Department and the matter is 
presently sub-judice in court. ISRO also informed that it has introduced e-payment and e-
procurement to bring in transparency and rule out scope for corruption. 
5.4 At the outset, the Committee congratulated ISRO on successful launch of India’s 
communication satellite GSAT -30 on 17 th January, 2020. The Committee was happy 
that ISRO, which is established in 1969, has been a source of pride for India. It has not 
only bagged achievement which others countries are yet to, it has also put India on the 
world map of space missions. 
5.5 On vigilance setup, the Committee  is of the view that corruption is a complex 
phenomenon involving officials, organizations both public and priv ate and public at 
large. Its roots may lie in an organization but the ramifications may extend beyond the 
boundaries of that organization. Therefore, the Committee recommends the 
Government to create an interface between the vigilance units of Central Gove rnment 
and its authorities, CPSUs, CPSBs and other bodies owned and controlled by the 
Central Government. The Committee is hopeful that such a platform will facilitate 
exchange of best practices, information and experiences. 
 
 
 

26 
 
General Recommendations: 
6.1 The Committee is of the opinion that in view of the extent of geographical spread 
and the scale of corruption in the country, the present vigilance set up is inadequate to 
handle the volume of work. The Committee therefore recommends that there is an 
imperative need to strengthen the vigilance administration with adequate manpower 
and requisite infrastructure including building up a robust surveillance system with 
certain amount of independence and autonomy so as to improve the effectiveness of 
vigilance administration and ensure expeditious disposal of cases. 
6.2 The Committee is of the view that surveillance is an integral part of vigilance, 
whether collecting intelligence about the corrupt practices committed or likely to be 
committed by the employees of  any organization or identifying areas vulnerable to 
corruption. At present, most organizations depend upon employees and informal 
sources for source information and intelligence about possible malpractices and 
misconduct among the employees of the organiz ation. In the absence of surveillance 
/intelligence unit, vigilance officers are over burdened with the dual responsibility of 
surveillance and vigilance administration. Therefore, the Committee recommends that a 
dedicated surveillance unit be set up in every organization for the purpose. 
6.3 The Committee also notes that over the years focus of organizations has shifted 
from punitive vigilance to preventive vigilance and organizations are increasingly using 
information and communication technologies such a s e -procurement, e -tendering, 
online grievance redressal mechanism to prevent the occurrence of lapses. The 
Committee is of the view that, quite often, individual employees don’t raise red flags 
and choose to remain mute spectators for fear of reprisal fro m the perpetrators. 
Therefore, the Committee desires that the feasibility of involving employees 
associations and trade unions in strengthening preventive and detective vigilance be 
explored. 
6.4 The Committee was informed that the post of CVO is an ex -cadre post initially 
appointed on deputation for three years which is extendable up to two years in the same PSU 
(total five years) or up to three years on transfer to another PSU on completion of initial 
tenure (3 years) in the previous PSU (i.e. total six y ears). Whereas, other Vigilance Officers 
are appointed from within the concerned PSUs, for a period of three years, keeping in view 
the sensitivity of the Vigilance wing and to avoid any vested interests.  
6.5 However, during the deliberations on the subject, some CMDs/CVOs had informed 
the Committee that the tenure of Vigilance Officers is short and inadequate, as much of the 
time  is spent on training and learning the nitty -gritty of this specialized job. Vigi lance 
Officers are selected from within the organization and since they lack exposure to the field 
of vigilance, these officials are trained through formal and on the job training. By the time 
these officials become well versed with their job, their tenure  is completed and they are 
repatriated to their original cadre. 
6.6 The Committee therefore recommends the Ministries  concerned to take all 
possible measures to ensure that successor CVO is appointed well before the incumbent 
CVO relinquishes charge. Furth er, considering the time spent on training and learning 
the job, the Committee recommends that the tenure of CVOs may be extended upto five 
years so as to  enable the organization to reap the benefits of the officers’ expertise in 
vigilance matters.  
 

27 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE - AT A GLANCE 
 
1. The Committee feels that the possibility of involving employees associations and 
trade unions in strengthening preventive vigilance should also be explored.  
(Para 2.13)  
 
2. The Committee notes that CVC in its report ‘TOP 100 BANKING FRAUDS’ 
presented a sector -wise analysis of frauds and their general modus operandi , 
loopholes in the existing system and suggested systemic improvements to plug 
them. The Committee impresses upon  the Ministries concerned to ensure that 
organizations under their jurisdiction carry out systemic improvements suggested 
by the Commission and strengthen fraud prevention mechanism to reduce the 
incidence of frauds.                            (Para 2.14)  
 
3. The Committee appreciates the constant endeavour of Central Vigilance 
Commission to bring in transparency, equity and competitiveness in procurement 
and contracting through promoting the adoption and implementation of integrity 
pact. The Committee notes that multiple benefits like improved transparency, 
image and reputation as an ethical organization;  reduced external interference, 
frivolous lawsuits and complaints from vendors;  speed up the Tenders 
Procurement Process; etc.  have been accrued to ONGC, whi ch is the first 
organization in India to implement Integrity Pact. The Committee therefore 
recommends that Integrity Pact is implemented in all government 
agencies/organization and it is strengthened as a tool of robust preventive vigilance 
mechanism.                                                     (Para2.16) 
 
4. The Committee hopes that Integrity Index is progressively extended to cover all 
Government organizations and it is implemented in a manner that it promotes a 
healthy competition among the organisations to climb up the ladder. 
(Para 2.18) 
 
5. In view of the above, the Committee feels that there is a dire need to revamp the 
current traini ng apparatus of CVOs and VOs in  PSUs/PSBs by promoting 
awareness about latest technologies. The Committee, ac cordingly, recommends  
CVC to prepare extensive training framework/modules for CVOs and VOs of 
PSUs/PSBs by giving due regard to their specific areas of operations.  The 
Committee also recommends CVC to revamp the existing training programme so 
as to enable  CVOs and vigilance officials to keep pace with changing times with 
focus on advanced technology and forensics.              (Para 2.20) 
 
6. The Committee is in complete agreement with the views of the Commission, and 
recommends that learning from the abovementioned short comings diagnosed by 
the commission, proactive steps are taken by PSUs/PSBs to avert recurrence of 
such frauds in future.  The PSUs, PSBs and Insurance Companies should put in 
place SOPs for all their activities, by clearly defining ro le, function and delegation, 
at all levels in the organization, leaving a minor or no role for use of discretion. 
                                                      (Para 2.22) 
 

28 
 
7. The Committee also observes that most scams and financial frauds unearthed in 
the country in recent times are transnational in character and involved round 
tripping of funds. Round tripping usually involves several layers of financial 
transactions and a maze of companies, banks and foreign investors, thus 
presenting a formidable challenge for the investigators to establish the money trail. 
In view of rising incidence of transnational crimes, the Committee recommends 
the investigating agencies to create a pool of dedicated investigators with 
significant expertise in forensic audit.                           (Para 2.23) 
 
8. Therefore, the Committee is of the considered view that a Centralised Database 
containing details of suspicious entities, fraudsters and their general modus 
operandi be created by collating data available with indivi dual organizations, 
regulators, investigating agencies as seamless sharing of such information among 
all the stakeholders concerned will bring down cases of all nature. 
(Para 2.24) 
 
9. The Committee is of the view that Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR), through 
which companies give back to the society, has the potential to uplift the living 
standards of the local population. But, usually,  companies spend the amount 
earmarked for CSR activities towards the development of their local township and 
infrastructure and for the benefit of the employees of the organisation and a very 
insignificant part of it is spent for the development of neighbourhood. The local 
population is by and large, deprived of benefits of CSR activities. The Committee 
feels that once the  Company’s CSR funds are streamlined towards the upliftment 
of local population, the activities such as pilferage might come down.  
                                (Para 2.26) 
 
10. The Committee therefore recommends that a provision for special allowance may 
be made for the CVOs, especially for those posted outside Delhi to effectively 
attract and retain talent.                            (Para 2.28) 
 
11. Further, the representatives of various bodie s brought to the notice of the 
Committee the plight of the officers working in the vigilance department. The 
Committee notes that officers working in Vigilance face delicate situation when 
they return to parent department as they have to work with colleagu es against 
whom they handled Vigilance case(s). This may affect their functioning and 
judgement in investigation. Hence, the Committee suggests CVC to ensure that at 
least 50% of the sanctioned strength of vigilance Department is drawn on 
deputation from other organization as far as practicable. 
(Para 2.29) 
 
12. However, the Committee is of the view that there is a little awareness about the 
procedure of filing complaint under PIDPI Resolution among the public. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends the Government to raise awareness about 
PIDPI Resolution through massive public outreach campaigns and wide publicity 
in the print, electronic media and also in social media which has emerged as a 
powerful participatory medium of communication in recent times. 
(Para 2.32) 
 

29 
 
13. Consequently, it was felt that the Act required amendments aimed at safeguarding 
against disclosures affecting sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the 
State, etc., before it is brought into force, the Government  introduced the Whi stle 
Blowers Protection (Amendment) Bill, 2015 in the Lok Sabha which was passed by 
the Lok Sabha on 13 th May, 2015. The said Bill was transmitted to the Rajya 
Sabha. However, due to dissolution of 16 th Lok Sabha, this amendment Bill needs 
to be re -introduced in the House.  The Committee hopes that the Whistle Blowers 
Protection (Amendment) Bill, 2015 may be introduced in the House without any 
further delay and passed by both the Houses.              (Para 2.34) 
 
14. In order to achieve this, the Committee recommends to employ such novel 
technologies as  Block Chain technology, Artificial Intelligence etc. to leave 
miniscule opportunity for misuse by unscrupulous elements. The Government and 
the CVC should work together with the RBI and Banks to overcome such  types of 
frauds by strengthening the existing system.                          (Para 2.35) 
 
15. To ensure accountability of TPEs, the Committee recommends that a Code of 
Conduct and a legally enforceable agreement should be executed by all these 
TPEs, so as to bring in better ethics and accountability on their part. 
(Para 2.36)  
 
16. The Committee is appreciative of the actions taken by CBDT to improve 
preventive vigilance in the Department particularly in terms of elimination of 
human interference and maximum use of technology. The Committee, however, 
observes that overdependence on these technological tools give rise to new forms of 
corruption which do not require in -person interaction such as digital bribery, 
blackmail on the basis of data, unauthorised access to digital information of 
taxpayers that corrupt tax officials may have.      (Para 3.4) 
 
17. The Committee feels that technology may also lead to complexity of official 
procedures and processes as officials and tax evaders who understand technology 
and systems may exploit it to their evil design. Lack of digital literacy or 
technological illiteracy also brings in middlemen having technological knowhow to 
use the vulnerabilities of the service seekers to extort bribes.  The Committee, 
therefore, feels that the CBDT should not fall prey to techno utopianism as  
technology is merely an advanced tool and is not a final solution to eradicate 
corruption in departments under the purview of CBDT and it is not always true 
that if human interference is reduced, corruption might go down as it is human 
beings only who operate these technological tools who on occasions may turn 
fallible.                                  (Para 3.5) 
 
18. The Committee is of the view that corruption is a big challenge in this country and 
it should be dealt with through various mechanisms. A robust vigilance 
mechanism shou ld be put in place as the level of corruption increases where 
surveillance and enforcement by public authority is weak. CBDT may consider 
appointing officers from other organisations on deputation in vigilance units of 
their organisation for a particular period as this would ensure relative impartiality 
of vigilance officers.  Besides, a service condition may be added in the Departments 
under purview of CBDT that officers who resign or retire from their services may 
not join private sector.                               (Para 3.6) 

30 
 
 
19. The Committee notes that, historically, personal interaction between tax officer 
and tax payer has been a major avenue for corruption. The Committee feels that 
faceless assessment will minimize opportunities for corruption by eliminating 
physical interface and person -to-person contact in the scrutiny assessments. The 
Committee appreciates CBDT for making all out efforts to ensure corruption free 
tax administration.                    (Para 3.7) 
 
20. The Committee recommends that a time frame should be put in place for refunds 
as it will ease things for assesses and if no refunds are made in the time frame, 
stern action should be taken against officers concerned. 
(Para 3.8) 
 
21. The Committee is aware that the officials who are charged with corruption take 
undue longer time in submitting replies against their charge sheets. The 
Committee is of the view that the time frame should be strictly followed in these 
cases and a clause sho uld be added that those who do not reply to their charge 
sheets in given time frame may be considered guilty of charges made.  
(Para 3.9) 
 
22. The Committee appreciates the punitive action taken by CBDT to compulsorily 
retire ‘dead wood’ from the Department as corrupt, errant and non - performing 
officials are burden to the organization and the exchequer. The Committee 
understands that this move was in line with Prime Minister’s Independence Day 
address at the Red Fort last year, where he announced that the ‘black sheep’ in the 
tax administration who may have misused their power by harassing honest 
taxpayers or taking excessive action for minor procedural violations will be 
removed. This action is also in line with the objectives of  incumbent Government 
to clean -up the bureaucracy. The Committee recommends that more punitive 
action is required to be done to improve the image of CBDT and a massive exercise 
should be undertaken in this regard.                                                           (Para 3.13) 
 
23. The Committee appreciates CBDT for making an all -out effort to augment tax 
collection in the country and bring tax evaders into the tax net. The Committee, 
however, feels that the Department should treat assesses as their asset s and follow 
good behavioural norms while conducting searches and raids. Tax Departments 
across the world have changed their stance towards taxpayers in terms of dealing 
with them which is to treat them as partners and clients rather than as tax 
evaders. T he Department should adopt corporate etiquettes of service industry 
and transform into a service-oriented organization.                                   (Para 3.16) 
 
24. The Committee is of the view that instead of high -handed, arrogant and rude 
conduct, the income tax sleuths should be well behaved and deal with the public 
with efficiency as well as decency as they are clients and partners of the 
department. Search operations during odd hours in night should also be avoided if 
there are no compelling reasons to do so. The department should have a policy of 
zero tolerance towards rude and arrogant conduct on the part of tax officials with 
taxpayers and for this the officials should be imparted training in soft skills so that 
they could be courteous and polite w hile dealing with taxpayers. The Committee 
recommends that errant officials should be penalized if they resort to such actions 

31 
 
even after repeated complaints and warnings. The need for remedy could not be 
more urgent.                                          (Para 3.17) 
 
25. Filing Income Tax returns is a cumbersome process, full of technicalities and 
therefore challenging. Sometimes, due to the complex nature of online forms, 
errors may creep in inadvertently. The Committee feels that law abiding taxpayers 
should be given an opportunity to rectify their returns.             (Para 3.18) 
 
26. The Committee is of the opinion that CBDT should always conduct its work in a 
neutral, non -partisan and non -discriminatory manner so that the Department 
could gain respect in the eyes of the general masses for its political neutrality and 
no one could accuse them of working under political pressures. Working of 
enforcement agencies under pressure  of those in power creates crisis for 
institutional autonomy and against the very s pirit of the concept of political 
neutrality of bureaucracy which may endanger the very fundamentals of 
democracy.                   (Para 3.21) 
 
27. The Committee takes note of the submission of CBIC in regard to the steps taken 
to strengthen preventive vigil ance in the Department as well as at ports, airports 
etc. through maximum use of advance technology and reducing human 
intervention. The Committee appreciates that the CBIC has taken various 
measures such as ICEGATE, E-SANCHIT, ICETRAK, E-Payment of Duty, APIS, 
DPE, SWIFT etc. to streamline fast movement of goods and services and to ensure 
robust preventive mechanism in the organisation.                                        (Para 4.6) 
 
28. The Committee also notes that there are scanning and examination facilities at 
ports of our country in which only 5 -10 per cent of the total containers per 
consignment are scanned and are picked up randomly by the system for scanning 
as ports have limited capacities for scanning. The Committee recommends that 
full-body or drive -through scanners should be installed in a phased manner at all 
the ports in such a way that trucks or other vehicles carrying containers can 
simply pass through these scanners and get fully scanned as has been done at some 
integrated check posts and ports in the country. This will ensure 100 per cent 
scanning. The Committee believes that after installation of the full body or drive 
through scanners at all the ports, the smuggling of c oncealed drugs, weapons and 
other contraband through the ports will be curbed. This will put an end to 
smuggling and subsequent revenue losses and criminal and terrorist activities.  
                                                                                         (Para 4.7) 
 
29. The Committee is also aware of the limitations of  scanners as they are manned by 
fallible officials who may fall prey to bribery as had happened during Mumbai 
bomb blast of 1993 in which some customs officials including an IRS officer had 
aided and abetted illegal imports of RDX and other weapons for the Mumbai 
bomb blast. In view of this, the Committee recommends that a fool proof vigilance 
set up should be put in place and stern actions should be taken action corrupt 
officials in a time bound manner as the involvement of corrupt officials in import 
or export of illegal items may not only cause revenue loss but also pose threat to 
national security. The Committee also recommends that CBIC may also  appoint 
officers on deputation from other organisations in their vigilance units as they, 

32 
 
being outsiders, may act in non -partisan manner during their limited tenure.                                                                                        
           (Para 4.8) 
 
30. The Committee is pleased to note that several steps have been taken by CBIC to 
punish errant, corrupt or non -performing officials of the organisations under its 
purview. The Committee also notes that CBIC has compulsorily retired such 
officials who gave a bad image to the organisation. This action is also in the line 
with the objectives of incumbent government to clean -up the rot in the 
bureaucracy. The Committee recommends that more punitive action is  required 
and a massive exercise should be taken up in t his regard at the earliest as it will 
give a strong message to other officials.                (Para 4.12) 
 
31. The Committee is aware of the fact that CBIC is helping the Government in terms 
of collection of taxes and being an important enforcement organizati on their 
invaluable contribution to the country, cannot be denied. However, the Committee 
is of the view that the officials should project an image of professional taxmen with 
etiquettes of service industry and instead of arrogant and rude conduct, they 
should be well behaved and deal with the public politely. The CBIC should have a 
policy of zero tolerance towards rude and arrogant conduct of tax officials and 
they should be imparted training in soft skills so that they could be courteous and 
polite while dealing with general public. The errant officials should be penalized if 
they resort to such actions even after repeated warning.             (Para 4.14) 
 
32. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the officials of CBIC should treat 
common Indian citizens returning from foreign tour as well as foreign tourists 
visiting India courteously and in a professional manner while performing their 
core job of searching for illegal contrabands. Indecent and feudal behaviour while 
conducting searches at airports dents the image of the department.  
(Para 4.15)

the agenda for the day i.e. (i) adoption of report on “ Effectiveness of Vigilance 
Administration in Central Government Ministries, Corporation, Societies, Public Sector 
Enterprises, etc” and recording of viewpoints of (ii) Shri Harish Narsappa, DAKSH and Shri 
Ameen Jauhar and Prashant Reddy, Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy on the subject

'Strengthening the Justice Delivery Process'. He then invited the Members to offer their views 
on the report so that it may be adopted. 
3.     Members deliberated on various issues pertaining to the report and raised issues relating 
to appointment procedures and posti ng of CBI and vigilance officers, prosecution of 
officials/CVOs of banks and institutions were fraud occurred, issue of Whistle Blowers 
Protection Bill etc. Thereafter, the Chairman assured the Members that Secretary, 
Department of Personnel and Training, Secretary, Department of Financial Services and 
other stakeholders will to be heard before the report is presented to the Parliament.  
(After arrival of the witnesses) 
4.       The Chairman welcomed the witnesses and requested Shri Harish Narsappa , DAKSH 
to take the floor followed by representatives of Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy.  
5.        Shri Harish Narsappa opined that the administrative work of judiciary is a part -time 
work carried out by respective Chief justice of High Courts and submitte d that judges should 
be relieved from administrative work by creating a separate specialized administrative cadre 
to manage administrative works of courts so that they can focus on judicial aspects. He added 
that the Parliament should enact a legislation t o create specialized administrative body as 
happened in some western countries. He also apprised the Committee of the non -
implementation of decisions of judiciary and added that also added that judiciary should be 
helped in implementing its decisions. He further added that uncertainty of case hearing due to 
frequent adjournments and non-scientific case listing in subordinate courts are major cause of 
pendency of cases. On the issue of optimal number of strength, he refuted the idea of judges -
population ratio and added that it should be based on cases filed, time spent by each judge 
and capacity of judges from subordinate courts onwards. 
6.      In addition to concurrence with the views of DAKSH, Ameen Jauhar, Senior Fellow, 
Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy apprised the Committee of their studies in mediation centres in 
Bangalore, Delhi and Allahabad and submitted that to strengthen justice delivery system 
standalone legislation on mediation is need of the hour to set out mediation pr ocess in India 
which should also look at aspects like regulation of mediation process, issues of accreditation 
and a centralized body to oversee its functioning. On the issue of All India Judicial Service, 
he added that if it is to be proposed the unique n ature of judiciary and subjective experience 
of each State may be taken into account during the selection of candidates. 
7.       Thereafter, Members  raised specific queries relating to increasing working hours of 
courts, judicial delay due to unpreparedne ss of lawyers, reducing frequent adjournments, 
interest of lawyers to be taken into account in the justice delivery system, wasting of time 
due to existing mediation process, rising cost of justice delivery, increasing judges strength 
and court infrastructure, registrars in courts to act as administrative officers to manage court 
affairs, All India Judicial service may violate principle of Article 233 of the Constitution of 
India, attachment of Family Courts with regular courts is against the Family Courts Act, low 
representation of minorities and backward sections in judiciary. 
8.       The Chairman, while summing-up, observed that judicial data is a prerequisite for any 
judicial reforms and proposed the creation of service like Information Utility Service as 
present in Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016  to offer genuine information relating to 
judiciary. He was also in agreement with the witne sses that Chief Justices are burdened by 
administrative works of courts from transfers to appointments. He was furthered concerned 
with the lack of IT infrastructure, DNA labs, forensic labs etc in dedicated courts. He was

also of the view that judicial de lay is also due to heard by Supreme Court becoming final 
authority, instead of cases disposing at High Court level.

CHAPTER - I 
Effectiveness of Vigilance Administration in Central Government Ministries, 
Corporation, Societies, Public Sector Enterprises, etc. 
 The Committee had interaction with the representatives Neyveli Lignite Corporation 
Ltd. (NLC), Chennai Petroleum Corporation Ltd. (CPCL) and United India Insurance 
Company Ltd (UIICL) at Chennai;  Life Insurance Corporation (LIC), Shippin g Corporation 
of India Ltd and Dena Bank at Mumbai; UCO Bank, Coal India Ltd. and Metal Scrap Trading 
Corporation Ltd. (MSTC) at Kolkata on the subject. Officers from the concerned 
Ministries/Departments and DoPT were also present in those meetings. 
2. The above mentioned PSUs/PSBs made a detailed presentations to the Committee 
inter-alia highlighting their internal vigilance mechanism, steps taken by them in 
strengthening vigilance administration, spreading awareness about vigilance amongst their 
stakeholders, etc. Following points were highlighted by the PSUs/PSBs in their presentation: 
 The Committee was apprised by the top management of the PSUs/PSBs that their 
focus has shifted from punitive to preventive vigilance. They have leveraged 
Information and Co mmunication Technology (ICT) for this purpose which inter -
alia includes online tendering, bill tracking, e -procurement, e -auction, online 
filing and tracking of complains, etc. The Committee was also apprised that 
because of these steps, taken over the yea rs, number of vigilance cases has gone 
down significantly. 
 Further, as a part of preventive vigilance, ‘vigilance awareness weeks’ are 
organized regularly and the employees, clients, vendors, public etc. are made 
aware by holding seminars/lectures and publ icizing it through workshops, radio, 
Whatsapp and SMS, etc. 
 Notice Boards have been displayed in all the Units, to sensitize the Public not to 
give bribe and to intimate demand of bribe to the Competent Authority. 
 Vigilance activities and Vigilance related  issues are being published through in -
house magazine. 
 Surprise inspections and audit of satellite offices are done on regular intervals to 
check any fraud at the cutting edge level.  
 Various Complaints were referred to CVC and CBI, for advice/ investigati on 
Provision for internal and external audit including internal inspection of all 
Offices of PSUs and PSBs. 
 Provision for property returns obtained from employees annually. 
 Establishment of robust online grievance reporting and redressal mechanism 
adopted by all PSUs/PSBs including development of in -house data vigilance 
module.

 All procurements as per CVC guidelines. E -Tendering process as well as Reverse 
Auction system in place. 
 
3. Several queries viz. implementation of policy of zero tolerance towards corruption, 
check on pilferage of goods at source and during transportation, requirement of dedicated 
cadre within the PSUs/PSBs for vigilance purpose, reasons for not having a full time CVOs 
for certain PSUs, impediments for whistle blower protection policy, etc. were raised by the 
Chairman and Members of the Committee, which were responded by the representatives of 
the PSUs/PSBs. On the presentation made by the PSUs/PSBs, the Members of the 
observations of the Committee on the issues raised in the meetings are enumerated as under:- 
 There is a need for adequate staffing of the Vigilance Wing/Department of PSUs 
so that they can fulfil their mandate properly. 
 As regard, the selection criteria for selection of Vigilance officers/personnel in the 
organization it was stressed upon that such criteria should be stringent and persons 
of impeccable integrity and sound knowledge should be appointed on such posts. 
 The PSUs may explore the possibility of having a full -fledged dedicated cadre of 
vigilance personnel to deal with vigilance cases. This will further help in 
improving vigilance administration in the organisation. It was felt the need for 
enhancing the tenure of Vigilance Officers which is at present 3 years t o at least 5 
years, as much of their time is spent on learning and training on vigilance 
machinery and issues.  
 Preventive vigilance, which signifies continuous watchfulness on the part of the 
top management, is the need of the hour. It was stressed on the  need to associate 
trade unions in vigilance administration especially preventive vigilance.  
 Promotion of whistle blower protection policy is not only extremely beneficial to 
the organisation and its employees, but also for its shareholders, society and t he 
nation at large.  
 As per the presentation made by PSUs/PSBs to the Committee, it was noted that 
the number of vigilance complaints made/registered is coming down significantly 
over the years. There may be two scenarios, either this might be due to the 
robustness of the vigilance administration in the organization or might also due to 
lack of people’s confidence in the vigilance setup of the organization to mitigate 
the problem. 
 As part of preventive vigilance many programmes like organizing vigilance 
awareness weeks, etc. are being carried out by PSUs/PSBs. But it was felt by the 
Committee that such awareness do not yield desired results. There is a need to 
rethink strategies for enhancing vigilance awareness among employees of the 
organization. 
 Pilferage of Coal at the mining site as well as during its transportation has been a 
big concern. The Committee was made to understand that one of the major causes 
of pilferage of Coal from the mining site by the local population is their abject 
poverty. The Member felt that Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR), which was 
introduced as company’s efforts to improve society in some way, has the potential 
to uplift the living standards of the local population. 
 NLC’s Vigilance Systems/Procedures has been certified by I SO 9001 -2015 
Quality Management Systems. All other PSUs should follow this example.  
 During the interaction with the PSUs/PSBs, it was observed that fraud and other 
malpractices still persists in certain areas of those undertakings, which is an 
indication of failure of internal vigilance mechanism. Thus all PSBs should take 
proactive steps to eradicate such malpractices completely.

(iii)  Investigation of Complaints & Initiation of appropriate remedial Action. 
(iv) Enhancing vigilance awareness and Compliance level among the employees

01.10.2018 and two Independent External Monitors (IEMs) were nominated. Quarterly 
Structured Meetings of IEMs with CVO & concerned Executives are conducted and Action 
Taken Report on the Minutes of the meetings is reviewed. Bank is also affec ting rotational 
transfers as per direction of CVC in respect of Officers who are continuing beyond 3 years 
from the sensitive seat / post and not necessarily from the station. It was further informed that 
the Annual Confidential Reports of CVO is written b y the MD & CEO and sent to the DFS, 
Ministry of Finance for review and for onward submission of the same to CVC as accepting 
authority. CVO and Vigilance Department officials also undergo periodical training 
programme for skill development. 
 
2.20 Andhra Bank further submitted that obviate undue delay in conduction and conclusion 
of CBI cases in view of the large number of such cases, the threshold limit for investigation 
of fraud cases by CBl may be increased from the present level of outstanding of Rs.3.00 Cr to 
a higher level which may be about Rs. 10 Cr or above. Further, it was also suggested that the 
realizable value of primary & collateral securities and probable cash recovery from other 
sources, if any, may be allowed to be deducted from the outstandi ng balance and on the 
remaining amount, up to about 50% provision may be made. This would enable Bankers to 
declare such accounts as Fraud without delay.   
2.21 The Committee notes that there are instances where unscrupulous borrowers/ 
middlemen raise high  value credit by   fudging financial statements, excess valuation of 
Primary & Collateral securities, obtaining clear legal opinion on defective documents in 
collusion with financial consultants/CA/Valuers/Advocates as the case may be. As Bankers 
generally depend on such professionals’ advice for decision making.  It is suggested that in 
all such cases, if the loans and advances turn NPA solely due to above reasons/ irregularities, 
Bank officials may not be held accountable for the accounts turning into NPA . Further, legal 
framework is to be strengthened to take punitive action on such professionals by implicating 
them in the CBI cases. Such measures may deter them from doing unscrupulous activities.  
2.22 In recent past many frauds have come to the notice o f Banks due to improper 
certification done by the TPEs and the Banks have failed to hold them accountable. To 
ensure accountability of TPEs, the Committee suggested that a Code of Conduct and a

4.22 On hearing all the four presentations, the Committee was of the opinion that in 
view of the extent of geographical spread and the scale of corruption in the country, the 
present vigilance set up seems to be inadequate to handle the volume of work. It feels 
that there is an imperative need to strengthen the vigilance administration with adequate 
manpower and requisite infrastructure including building up a robust surveillance system 
so as to improve the effectiveness of vigilance administration and ensure expeditious 
disposal of cases. 
4.23 The Committee was also of the view that cor ruption is a complex phenomenon 
involving officials, organizations both public and private and public at large. Its roots 

70 
 
may lie in an organization but the ramifications may extend beyond the boundaries of 
that organization. Therefore, the Committee recom mends the Government to create an 
interface between the vigilance units of Central Government and its authorities, CPSUs, 
CPSBs and other bodies owned and controlled by the Central Government. The 
Committee is hopeful that such a platform will facilitate e xchange of best practices, 
information and experiences.

and Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. ( ONGC), IRCON and Rashtriya  Chemical

5. On this last leg of the study tour, the Committee requested all the representatives of 
PSBs/PSUs, to combine their presentation and highlight the main points pertaining to the 
vigilance administration before the  Committee due to paucity of time as large number of 
stakeholders is were scheduled to be heard by the Committee. Following points were 
highlighted by the PSUs/PSBs in their presentation: 
 
 The Committee was apprised by the top management of the PSUs/PSBs t hat their 
focus has shifted from punitive to preventive vigilance. They have leveraged 
Information and Communication Technology (ICT) for this purpose which inter-alia 
includes online tendering, bill tracking, e -procurement, e -auction, online filing and 
tracking of complains, etc. The Committee was also apprised that because of these 
steps, taken over the years, number of vigilance cases has gone down significantly. 
 
 Further, as a part of preventive vigilance, ‘vigilance awareness weeks’ are organized 
regularly and the employees, clients, vendors, public etc. are made aware by holding 
seminars/lectures and publicizing it through workshops, radio, whatsapp and SMS, 
etc. 
 
 Notice Board has been displayed in all the Units, to sensitize the Public not to give 
bribe and to intimate demand of bribe to the Competent Authority. 
 
 Vigilance activities and Vigilance related issues are being published through in -house 
magazine. 
 
 Surprise inspections and audit of satellite offices are done on regular intervals to 
check any fraud at the cutting edge level.  
 
 Various Complaints were referred to CVC, CBI, PMO, etc. Provision for internal and 
external audit including internal inspection of all Offices of  the respective PSUs and 
PSBs. 
 
 Provision for property returns obtained from employees annually. 
 
 Establishment of robust online grievance reporting and redressal mechanism adopted 
by all PSUs/PSBs including development of in-house data vigilance module. 
 
 All procurements as per CVC guidelines. E -Tendering process as well as Reverse 
Auction system in place. 
 
5.1 The Committee noted that corruption is a complex and intricate web of acts of 
interaction and reciprocity and is the outcome of nexus between Government officials, 
private sector and public at large. Vigilance, thus, cannot be confined to a set up. Therefo re, 
the Committee suggested that the radar of vigilance be expanded to cover Intra 
Organizational Vigilance -Vigilance on the employees of the organization; Inter 
Organizational Vigilance -Vigilance on transactions/areas of interaction between 

71 
 
organizations; and Extra Organizational Vigilance -Vigilance on transactions/areas of 
interaction between organizations and general public, private individuals and any other 
stakeholders.

REPORT 
CHAPTER-I 
VIRTUAL COURTS 
1.1 World over, the COVID-19 pandemic has forced Courts to get creative to continue to 
execute their duties. Courts had to explore ways and means to become less dependent on 
physical appearances and more receptive to online  options. Virtual Courts have now become 
the primary or the only means for dispensation of justice. 
History of Virtual Courts 
1.2 One of the earliest references to Virtual Courts can be found in the works of Professor 
Frederick I Lederer who is currently t he Director, Centre for Legal and Court Technology, 
United states. He wrote in 1997- 
‘The Courtroom is a place of adjudication, but it is also an information 
hub. Outside information is assembled, sorted and brought into the Courtroom 
for presentation. Onc e presented, various theories of interpretation are argued 
to the fact finder who then analyses the data according to prescribed rules 
(determined by the judge through research, analysis and interpretation) and 
determines a verdict and result. The Courtroo m is thus the centre of a complex 
system of information exchange and management. Ultimately because lawyers 
and judges deal continuously with ‘data’, high technology Courtrooms exist and 
Virtual Courtrooms are possible.’ 
1.3 Lederer, as far back as in 1997, with an impressive degree of foresight, predicted how 
digital technologies transform the legal landscape in future. Given the pace and the degree of 
digital incursion into almost all facets of human activity, it is clear that technology will 
become an omnipresent feature of the Courtroom. 
The Great Debate 
1.4 Any discussion on Virtual Courts revolves around a central question - Is Court a place 
or a Service? The advocates of Virtual Courts argue that Court is a Service and not a place. A 
bird’s eye view of various definitions of ‘Court’ helps resolve the debate. 
1.5 As far as India is concerned, neither the Civil and Criminal Procedural Codes nor the 
General Clauses Act embodies the definition of the term ‘Court’. However, as per the legal 
glossary of the Legislative Department, Ministry of Law and Justice, ‘Court’ is a place where 
justice is administered. Further, Section 3 of the Evidence Act, defines 'Court' as follows: 
'Court includes all Judges and Magistrates and all persons, except arbitrators, legall y 
authorized to take evidence. In Section 20 of the Indian Penal Code, 'Court of Justice' is 
defined as a judge, who is empowered by law to act judicially alone, or a body of judges 
which is empowered by law to act judicially as a body, when such judge or body of judges is 
acting judicially.' 
1.6 The US Federal Judiciary defines ‘Court’ as a Government entity authorized to 
resolve legal disputes. Black’s Law dictionary defines ‘Court’ as governmental body 
consisting of one or more judges who sit to adjudica te disputes or as a place where justice is 
judicially administered. 

2 
 
1.7 From the above, it is clear that although the definition of Court varies across 
jurisdictions, they all seem to have two elements in common -That Court is a Government 
entity comprising one or more judges and that Court deals with the administration of Justice 
thus making it clear that Court is more of a Service than a place. 
How are Virtual Courts different from regular Courts? 
1.8 In Virtual Courts, Plaint and other documents are filed  electronically, arguments are 
heard over videoconferencing/teleconferencing, evidence is submitted digitally, judges decide 
cases online either presiding from the physical Courtroom or sitting in some other place. 
Thus, Virtual Courts transform the documentation, evidential and procedural mechanisms and 
conduct hearings online from start to finish. 
Virtual Courts, Online Courts, Online Dispute Resolution- THE DIFFERENCE: 
1.9 The Committee has observed that the terms Virtual Court, Online Court, and Online 
Dispute Resolution are being used interchangeably. Richard Susskind in his famous book 
titled ‘Online Courts and the Future of Justice’ has explained the differences among these 
terms clearly. 
1.10 In Virtual Courts , Plaint and other documents such as vala klatnama, written 
submissions are filed electronically; Court fees are paid electronically; Evidence is submitted 
digitally; arguments are heard over videoconferencing; witnesses give their testimony 
remotely over videoconferencing and Judge decides the ca se online either presiding from the 
physical Courtroom or from some other place. A copy of the Order/Judgement is made 
available on the website of the Court or through some electronic means. 
1.11 Online Courts  constitute an advancement over Virtual Courts.  The only difference 
between Virtual Courts and Online Courts being that in the former hearing is synchronous 
and the latter involves asynchronous form of interaction. This means that, in Virtual Court 
hearings, the Judge, advocates, litigants and witnesse s need to be available at the time of 
hearing for a case to progress. In contrast, in Online Courts, the participants need not be 
present simultaneously; arguments, evidence are presented to the Judge without the parties 
being together at the same time. 
1.12 Online Dispute Resolution refers to the use of online platforms for the resolution of 
disputes between parties through Alternative Dispute Resolution Mechanisms.  
International experience 
1.13 Virtual Courts are not a new phenomenon. Many countries have  adjudicated cases 
ranging from low value civil disputes to complicated criminal cases Virtually without 
advocates, litigants and witnesses having to set foot physically in the Courtroom. 
United States 
1.14 In United States, many State Courts have either installed webcast equipment or have 
Virtual Courtrooms. Mc Glothin Court room, set up by The Centre for Legal and Court 
Technology at the College of William and Mary Law School in Virginia is the world’s most 
technologically advanced trial and appellate Courtroom. 
Singapore  
1.15 The Singapore Supreme Court has successfully set up a Virtual Courtroom known as 
"The Technology Court", which has a Local Area Network (LAN) with an Internet 
connection and which allows the use of imaging, multimedia and video con ferencing. It also 

3 
 
has a Litigation Support System for Presentation (LSSP), a Computer Based Recording 
Transcription System (CBRT), a sophisticated audio visual system (AVS) which allows 
various types of audio and video information to be presented with eas e and a video 
conferencing to allow foreign witnesses to give evidence in any proceedings. The Supreme 
Court Infokiosk System (SCIS) which has touch sensitive screen and allows a user to obtain 
information on hearing schedules, the location of counter serv ices in the Supreme Court and 
to call up a multimedia floor directory of the Supreme Court complex.  
Turkey 
1.16 Turkey has a national e -judiciary system called UYAP. UYAP, which won the UN’s 
Public Service Award in 2012, has significantly increased the effectiveness and accessibility 
of the judicial system in Turkey, by providing faster, more transparent and more cost efficient 
judicial services than ever before. UYAP links together all judicial institutions in Turkey and 
it provides the possibility for the whole judicial process to be carried out through an 
electronic document flow. The system currently has 1.9 mill ion users, and it has resulted in 
annual savings of approximately 100 million USD, as well as significant environmental 
benefits, as it allows for a virtually paperless working environment. UYAP is complemented 
by an advanced video -conferencing service, wh ich allows for testimony and hearings to be 
carried out at distance, without having to transfer prisoners and detainees to Court.   
Canada 
1.17 In Canada, videoconferencing technology has been used to receive witness testimony 
in civil trials for over a de cade. The Ontario Rules of Civil Procedure allow for witnesses in 
civil trials to testify remotely using videoconference technology. 
Italy  
1.18 Italy has an “On -line Civil Trial” facility which covers all civil cases throughout the 
country. The system allows for an entirely electronic processing of cases, which significantly 
reduces the time and expenses related to accessing the Court. It integrates several high -
security features, including a two -stage authentication, digital signature, and certified email s. 
The system has 6 million daily users and it has resulted in annual savings of 55 million EUR. 
Virtual Courts and India 
1.19 The unpredictable lockdown caused by the corona virus pandemic has brought forth a 
crisis which affected human lives and also cri ppled the functioning of Indian Judiciary. In 
order to adjudicate urgent matters and to enable the judicial system to discharge its 
constitutional mandate of providing access to justice at all times, the Supreme Court of India 
has rolled out Virtual Court hearings. 
1.20 During the pre -COVID period, the VC set up was primarily used for conducting 
remand matters to prevent movement of prisoners between Courts and jails. Such VC 
facilities have been operationalized between 3240 Court complexes and correspondin g 1272 
prisons. 
1.21 Legal sanctity was given to videoconferencing by the Supreme Court by an 
overarching order invoking Article 142 of the Constitution of India passed on 6 th April 2020 
which covered all the High Courts in the country. Consistent with the peculiarities of the 
judicial system in every state and in view of the dynamic health situation, the High Courts 
were left with the discretion of adopting technology after cu stomisation to suit their purpose. 
Model rules on Video Conferencing have been circulated and the High Courts are in the 

4 
 
process of adopting them. The District Courts were to adopt the mode of video conferencing 
prescribed by the concerned High Court.
