Action Taken 
6.1 All India Service Officers (AIS): The recommendation is aligned to the extant Rules. 
All the state cadres will once again be requested to take timely action for review of the 
performance of AIS officers as per Rule 16(3) of The AIS (DCRB) Rules. 
6.2 Central Civil Services Employees: The Appropriate Authority has the absolute right 
to retire a Governmentservant under FR 56(J), FR 56(I) or Rule 48 (1) (b) of CCS (Pension) 
Rules, 1972 as the case may be, if it is necessary to do so in public interest to strengthen the 
administrative machinery by developing responsible andefficient workers at all levels and 
efficiency, economy and speed in the disposal of Government functions. 
6.3 Government has noted the recommendation of the Committee for undertaking rev iew 
of the performance of the Government servants on regular basis, without any bias and 

8 
 
favouritism. In this regard, instructions have been issued by the Government from time to 
time, requiring the appointing authorities to carry out periodical review of the performance of 
the Central Government servants. All these guidelines/instructions have been placed in public 
domain. Further, these guidelines inter-alia provide that such reviews are to be undertaken in 
each quarter of the year for cases falling due in subsequent six months. The guidelines further 
provide that after carrying out the review, based on the overall personal records of the officer, 
and not confined to Annual Performance Appraisal Report alone, an officer can be 
prematurely retired, on the g rounds of inefficiency and doubtful integrity. Further, 
instructions have also been issued from time to time, inter alia, highlighting the observations 
made by various Courts in the matter. These guidelines provide an enabling framework for 
removal of deadwood, as also to eliminate bias and favouritism while deciding the cases and 
to promote efficiency in the Government.  
6.4  Central Secretariat: The review of performance of the officers is undertaken 
periodically under FR 56 (j). In CSS cadre, one officer each in the grades of Director, Deputy 
Secretary, Under Secretary and Assistant Section Officer was retired under FR 56 (j) during 
past five years.

non-performers and of doubtful integrity during past five years and none has been 
prematurely retired on the basis of non -performance and doubtful integrity. CSCS is a

4.0 The Committee notes that appointments made through Lateral Entry are contractual

Recommendation/Observation 
5.0 The Committee notes that 360 degree performance appraisal intends to capture the 
qualities of officers in terms of integrity, capability and general reputation based on an 
appraisal of the Annual Performance Appraisal Report (APAR) by an Expert Committee and 
feedback received from various stakeholders. The Committee notes that such a system of 
empanelment has widened representation in the Central Government to all services. It has 
also eliminated discretion and scope for lobbying associated with senior level positio ns. 
However, the Committee notes that feedback in this process is obtained informally leaving it 
susceptible to manipulations. The Committee observes that the feedback received from 
subordinates and stakeholders may sometimes be biased and can lack objecti vity, 

18 
 
particularly if the officer had an occasion to discipline his subordinate or he was unable to 
meet the unjustified demands of stakeholders. The Committee recommends that the 
Government should take steps to ensure that such biased feedback is not reli ed upon in order 
that honest and deserving civil servants are not victimized.                                    (Para 3.27) 
Action Taken 
5.1 Multi Source Feedback from relevant stakeholders in Empanelment process (360* 
performance appraisal):- The Multi Source Feedback (MSF) system has been introduced with 
an aim at ensuring comprehensive assessment of officers for empanelment to hold senior 
positions in Government. Under it, officers are assessed by an Experts Panel (EP) not only on 
the basis of their ACR/APAR grades but also based on a feedback obtained from a minimum 
of 05 stakeholders including Seniors, Juniors, Peers, External Stakeholders and serving 
Secretaries. MSF is taken on seven clearly defined attributes which include decision making, 
ownership, pro-activeness, delivery, leadership, honesty and suitability for higher positions. 
In case of large variation between feedbacks of stakeholders, the EP may take more feedback 
from additional stakeholders. In addition, overall service record and vigilan ce inputs, etc. 
about the officers are also taken into account. Feedback from a diverse range of stakeholders 
and anonymity and confidentiality in the process ensures objectivity and transparency. 
 
5.2 In order to ensure fairness and objectivity in the process, assessment is done by the EP 
comprising four/five carefully chosen members of very high merit and integrity. The 
feedback obtained by the EP is appended to the final report thus, making it a well -
documented record rather than an informal process.  
5.3 A system of review is in place for officers not empanelled. In such cases, review is 
done by a separate panel of Experts, who obtain fresh MSF from a different set of 
stakeholders. 
5.4 Thus, it may be seen that feedback from diverse range of stakeholders  and anonymity 
and confidentiality in the process under MSF system ensures objectivity, transparency and 
fairness in the empanelment process.

Recommendation/Observation 
9.0 The Committee is of the view that civil servants should act in the best interest of the 
public at all times. Though there are laws, Institutions and mechanisms in place to curb 
corruption, it is increasingly being realised that such mechanisms alone are not sufficient to 
instill integrity in them. Thus, the Committee strongly feels that Civil servants should be 
sensitised about ethics and values in pub lic life through training. The Committee 
recommends LBSNAA to recalibrate its course content so as to make civil servants ethical 
and responsible in both interpersonal and intrapersonal realms. The Committee recommends 
LBSNAA that the measures taken to ins till ethics and values in public life in civil servants 
through training may be submitted to the Committee in its Action Taken Note.         
                                                                              (Para 5.3) 
Action Taken 
9.1 The mission of the LBSNAA is ‘To promote good governance by providing quality 
training for building a professional and responsive civil service in a caring, ethical and 
transparent framework’.   In keeping with this mission, it is the constant endeavour of the 
Academy to include the following core values of the Academy in all the inputs in different 
courses being administered here: 
(i)  Serve the Underprivileged : Be humane in your approach while dealing with 
people; be the voice of the underprivileged and be  proactive in addressing any injustice 
against them. You can achieve success in this endeavor if you act with integrity, respect, 
professionalism and collaboration. 
 
(ii) Integrity: Be consistent in your thoughts, words and actions which will make you 
trustworthy. Have courage of conviction and always speak the truth to even the most 
powerful, without fear. Never ever tolerate any degree of corruption, be it in cash, kind or 
intellectual. 
 
(iii) Respect: Embrace diversity of caste, religion, colour, gen der, age, language, region,

12.0 The Committee notes that Tribunals were established with the objective to provide 
speedy and inexpensive justice to the litigants. However, the level of  pendency in CAT puts 
across a serious point that this basic object of overcoming delays in dispensation of justice is 
far from being achieved. Hence, the Committee recommends the Government to identify the 
root causes of piling up of cases in tribunals an d apprise the Committee of the measures 
taken to cut the backlog of pending cases in the Action Taken note.                        (Para 6.21) 
Action Taken 
12.1 The Central Administrative Tribunal is a quasi -judicial body, created under the 
Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985, for the adjudication or trial by Administrative Tribunals 
of disputes and complaints with respect to recruitment and conditions of service o f persons 
appointed to public services and posts in connection with the affairs of the Union or of any 
local or other authority brought under its jurisdiction under section 14(2) of the Act.  
 
12.2 At present, the Tribunal exercises jurisdiction over the Departments of Government of 
India, Union Territories and 214 Boards, Corporation and Societies owned or controlled by 
the Government of India. The Central Administrative Tribunal has 07 regular Benches and 21 
Circuit Benches all over India. 
 
12.3 Since 1985 till December, 2019 about 8,14,796 cases have been instituted and out of 
these, 7,65,831 cases have already been disposed of, which is about 94% of the cases 
instituted during the period. Despite the shortage of Members, 26,040 cases have been 
disposed of against the 24,952 cases instituted during the year 2019, which is about 104.36% 
of the cases instituted during the said period.  
 
12.4 The primary reason of pendency of cases is that decision to be passed by higher courts 
(High Courts and Supreme Court) in similar cases are being awaited by Hon’ble CAT to pass 
decision in large number of similar pending cases. 
 
12.5 Also, another major reason is the vacancies of Members in the Tribunal. As on date, 
there are a total of 27 vacancies of Members (14 -Judicial and 13 -Administrative). For the 
vacancy year 2018, offer of appointment of 06 new Administrative Members have already 
been issued. One of them has assumed the charge of the office. On assumption of charge by 
other 05 Administrative Members, the number of vacancies will come down to 22.  
 
12.6 The process of filling up the vacancies for the year 2019 got deferred due to re -
formulation of the rules made under the Finance Act 2017. The Tribunal, Appellate Tribunal 
and other Authorities (Qualifications, Exper ience and other Conditions of Service of 
Members) Rules, 2020 have recently been notified on 12.02.20 under the Finance Act, 2017 
on implementation of Hon’ble Supreme Court’s judgment dated 13.11.19 passed in Civil 
Appeal No.  8588/2019 (Roger Mathew Vs So uth Indian Bank Ltd. & Others). Now, the 
advertisement for inviting applications for the vacancies of Members (CAT) for the vacancy 
year 2019 will be issued shortly.  
 
12.7 It is also to be placed on record that the functioning of the Tribunal is different  than 
those of other regular Courts, where Benches can be constituted by any two Judges. Here in 
the Tribunal, a Division Bench could only be constituted of one Judicial and one 

25 
 
Administrative Member. Thus, the deficiency in either category hampers the fun ctioning of 
the Tribunal. 
 
12.8 The Hon’ble Chairman is closely monitoring the disposal of Benches and also 
impressing upon to make every endeavour to reduce backlog pendency.  
 
12.9 It may be worth mentioning that implementation of Advance Case Informatio n 
System (ACIS) in CAT, which facilitates E -courts facility and includes e -filing, online 
remittance of fee, hearing of the cases through video conferencing at the discretion of the 
Tribunal is currently under progress. Once the ACIS will be operational, M embers of 
different Benches may constitute a Division Bench and hear the cases through video 
conferencing, which may be helpful to reduce the pendency of old cases to some extent.   
Further Observation 
12.10 The Committee has noted the reply of the Ministr y and hopes that Advanced 
Case Information System is operationalized soon.

ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES: 
Recommendation/Observation 
12.0 The Right of Citizens for Time -bound Delivery of Goods and Services and Redressal 
of their Grievances Bill, 2011 is essentially citizen centric and will ensure time bound 
delivery of Goods and services as well as facilitate timely redressal of grievan ces besides 
strengthening accountability and promoting transparency. The Committee in its 95th Report 
recommended the Government to consider the reintroduction of the said Bill and till then 
implement the proposed scheme without any further delay. The Comm ittee reiterates its 
earlier recommendation.                    (Para 7.12) 
Action Taken 
12.1 A CoS note on Delivery of Services and Grievances Redressal Scheme was referred 
to the Cabinet Secretariat. The proposal is being examined in consultation with the concerned 
authorities for appropriate action.  However, DARPG has taken the following measures to 
improve effectiveness of service delivery and grievance redressal: 
Service Delivery:  DARPG in its efforts to provide more responsive and citizen -
friendly governance coordinates with the Central Ministries to formulate and 
operationalise Citizen’s Charters.   Recently the Ministry has undertaken certain 
steps on Citizen Charter of Ministry of External Affairs and Central Board of 
Direct Taxes to review their Citizen’s Charters.  Based on this, the charter of both 
the organizations have been revamped to make them one stop information 
platform. DARPG is regularly  taking meetings with   Ministries on review and 
updation of their Citizen’s Charter. 
Public Grievances: DARPG has initiated the CPGRAMS Reforms by process re -
engineering of existing CPGRAMS for faster and qualitative resolution of 
grievances. The CPGRAMS 7.0 facilitate direct mapping of grievances with  last 
mile  officer  responsible for resolution to r educe the   disposal time , enable 
automatic escalation of the grievance to the next higher level if not resolved by the 
sub-ordinate office within the stipulated timeframe and  enable better identification 
of gaps between policy and delivery. 
12.2 The reform has already been implemented in 9 Ministries / Departments - Department 
of Posts, Telecom, DFS (Banking & Insurance), M/ Road Transport and Highways, M/ 
External Affairs, D/ School Education and literacy, M/ Health & FW and M/ Petroleum.   
Dept. of Posts reported that CPGRAM reforms have covered 1.5 lac post offices, saving 2323 
Mondays and reduced timelines of disposal substantially. 

40 
 
12.3 The reform would be implemented in all other Ministry/Departments/Organizations in 
phased manner. 
12.4 Further NIC has  developed web APIs to facilitate integration of State Grievance 
Portals with CPGRAMS. 8 States portals have been integrated so far.  
Further Observation  
12.5 The Committee is appreciative of the initiatives taken by DARPG to improve 
service delivery and facilitate speedy redressal of grievances. However, the Committee 
observes that the Ministry has avoided giving any reply in respect of the 
recommendation made by the Committee for reintroduction of the Right of Citizens for 
Time-bound Delivery of Goods an d Services and Redressal of their Grievances Bill, 
2011. The Committee reiterates its recommendation as it believes that passage and 
enactment of this bill will ensure time bound delivery of Goods and services and 
facilitate timely redressal of grievances for citizens and strengthen accountability and 
promote transparency. The Committee would like to be apprised of the view of the 
Ministry in this regard.

therefore, is of the view that not enough is being done to fill up the backlog 
vacancies and recommends that the DoPT should impress upon all the 
Ministries/Departments to take such steps as they deem proper to address the 
malaise.                       (Para 2.9) 
 
34. The Committee feels that as regards to All India Services, as per the extant rules, 
the reporting officers are required to recommend domain assignment for the 
officer reported upon. However, the Committee has a different view in this regard. 
The Committee is of the view that such an issue should not be left to the discretion 
of the reporting officer. The Committee recommends that the educational, 

45 
 
professional, regional, social, cultural background of the officer should be given 
primacy while considering h is or her domain of choice. Besides, the officer should 
have the leeway to decide the domain of his or her choice as per his or her self -
assessment of knowledge, skills, expertise and competence. Therefore, the 
Committee reiterates that there should be gro uping/ clusterisation of Ministries 
and assignment of officers to clusters of their choice based on their interest, 
aptitude and inclination.         (Para 3.6) 
 
35. The Committee had desired to be apprised about the status of compliance of the 
338 IAS officer s who hadn’t filed Immovable Property Returns in the preceding 
year; however, the Ministry has avoided furnishing the details. The Committee 
reiterates that a status note on the IAS officers who hadn’t filed Immovable 
Property Returns till date along with the reasons and action taken against such 
officers, be furnished to the Committee at the earliest.     (Para 4.7) 
 
36. The Committee further recommends that a detailed study should be conducted by 
an expert committee to assess the impact of the drastic changes  brought about by 
the Commission in the scheme of examination since 2010 both on the 
administration and on the candidates level, who were impacted by such changes.  
            (Para 5.6) 
 
37. The Committee would further like to be apprised of the details in re gard to 
number of candidates’ background wise (rural/urban)and language wise 
(English/Hindi/other vernacular taken as a medium of examination) selected by 
UPSC between 2005-10 and between 2010-2018.                                       (Para 5.7) 
 
38. The Committee is not satisfied with the response of the Ministry and recommends 
that the Ministry should impress upon the Finance Ministry to allocate additional 
funds to ISTM as per projection at RE stage so that they could recruit permanent 
staff against  vacancies. The Committee is also not satisfied with the reply of the 
Ministry as no concrete action plan in regard to filling up of almost 40 percent of 
vacant faculty positions have been furnished.  The Committee is of the view that 
the ISTM is a premier  training institution and it cannot be run with guest faculty. 
The Committee recommends that the ISTM should be adequately staffed and fund 
should not be a constraint in this regard. The Committee hopes that all the vacant 
positions will be filled up during this financial year.                           (Para 6.4) 
 
39. The Committee recommends that adequate funds should be provided to IIPA so 
that it can discharge its mandate effectively. The Committee recommends the 
Department to pursue with the Ministry of Fi nance to allocate additional funds to 
IIPA as per its projected demand at RE stage as any shortfall in allocation will 
adversely affect IIPA’s capacity to invest in training and research.   (Para 7.2) 
 
40. The Committee has noted that Rs 781.01 Cr was allocated to CBI in BE 2019 -20, a 
marginal increase from Rs 778.93 Cr allocated in 2018 -19. Again, only Rs. 802.79 
Cr have been allocated to CBI against the projected demand of Rs. 1386.26 Cr. 
The Committee und erstands that the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), a 
premium investigating arm of the Government investigates large number of 
sensitive, high -profile corruption and economic fraud cases against public 
servants, private persons, firms. Besides this, C BI also probes and pursues several 

46 
 
extradition cases against fugitive economic offenders as well as criminals in courts 
of other countries. Such investigation and probes require large scale deployment of 
human resources and funds. The Committee hopes that additional funds will be 
provided to the premier investigation agency at RE stage so that it can discharge 
its tremendous responsibilities without any hindrance.                (Para 8.2) 
 
41. The Committee has noted the reply of the Ministry. The Committee in  its previous 
Reports including its 95 th Report on Demands for Grants (2018 -19) had expressed 
its displeasure over slow pace of utilisation of funds by CBI. The Committee noted 
that  on account of underutilisation or slow pace of utilization of funds , allocations 
to CBI were reduced at the RE stage and consequently the Budget Estimates of 
next year are also reduced and it happened this financial year also. The 
Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that a robust monitoring mechanism 
should be set up in the organisation to monitor the pace of implementation of 
schemes and projects from start to finish and consequently proper utilisation of 
funds is ensured.           (Para 9.2) 
 
42. The Committee is not satisfied with the plain reply of the Ministry. The Committee 
is of the view that The Centralised Technology Vertical (CTV) project, which aims 
to facilitate real-time information sharing with investigators across the country, is 
an important project of CBI and it should be operationalized at the earliest. 
Besides this,  International Centre of Excellence in Forensic Science and 
International Centre of Excellence in Investigation should also be established soon. 
The Committee should be apprised of the steps taken for completion of both the 
projects and hurdles being faced by the Ministry in this regard.              (Para 10.2) 
 
43. The Committee takes note of the reply of the Ministry delineating the progress 
made with regard to addressing the problems of infrastructure and human 
resource deficits nagging CAT Infrast ructure Deficit. The Committee also takes 
note of the fact that out of seventeen benches, only eight benches are functioning 
from their own buildings, four benches are functioning from Government 
buildings and rest five Benches are functioning from rented buildings. The 
Committee is of the considered view that all nine benches including those which 
are functioning from Government buildings on rent or otherwise should have their 
own buildings and all necessary steps such as identification of sites, construct ion of 
buildings etc should be completed in time bound manner, however, priority should 
be given to benches which are functioning from rented buildings.           (Para 11.6) 
 
44. The Committee further notes that out of 66 sanctioned posts of Hon’ble Chairman/ 
Members (33 -Judicial and 33 -Administrative) 27 posts (14 -Judicial & 13 -
Administrative) of Hon’ble Members are vacant in various Benches and more 
vacancies are likely to arise this year. The Committee strongly recommends that 
all the vacancies should be fi lled up on priority basis at the earliest to reduce 
arrears and backlogs of cases.                                                  (Para 11.7) 
 
45. The Committee is appreciative of the initiatives taken by DARPG to improve 
service delivery and facilitate speedy redressal of grievances. However, the 
Committee observes that the Ministry has avoided giving any reply in respect of 
the recommendation made by the Committee for reintroduction of the Right of 
Citizens for Time -bound Delivery of Goods and Services and Redressal of their 

47 
 
Grievances Bill, 2011. The Committee reiterates its recommendation as it believes 
that passage and enactment of this bill will  ensure time bound delivery of Goods 
and services and facilitate timely redressal of grievances for citizens and 
strengthen accountability and promote transparency. The Committee would like 
to be apprised of the view of the Ministry in this regard.                         (Para 12.5)

REPORT 
 The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the 
Ministry of Law and Justice on the recommendations/observations of the Department -
related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and 
Justice contained in its One Hundred First Report on the Demands for Grants (2020 -
21) of the Ministry. The Report was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of 
Lok Sabha on the 6th March, 2020.  
2. The Committee had made as many as 54 recommendations/observations in its 
One Hundred First Report. Replies of the Ministry of Law and Justice thereto have 
been categorized and scrutinized under four chapters on the basis of satisfaction of the 
Committee. Final replies in respect of three recommendations/observations are 
awaited from Departments of the Ministry. Further, five paras i.e., para nos. 2.12, 
2.28, 3.56, 3.67, and 5.20 of the report on the Demand for Grants (2020 -21), Ministry 
of Law and Justice relates to general observations of the Committee on the 
functioning of Departments/Supreme Court of India/Election Commission of India. 
Out of 46 recommendations where final replies have been received as many as 26 (57 
percent approximately) of total recommendations are satisfactory. 
3. The recommendations/observations of  the Committee have been accepted by 
the Ministry contained under paras 2.36, 2.39, 2.59, 3.14, 3.18, 3.27, 3.31, 3.39, 3.46, 
3.55, 3.68, 4.11, 4.13 and 5.4 of the Report. The Committee is pleased to note that the 
Ministry has accepted its recommendations.  Those are dealt under Chapter -I of the 
Report. 
4. The recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to 
pursue in view of the replies given by the Ministry relates to paras 2.11, 2.44, 2.51, 
3.28, 3.64, 3.65, 4.17, 4.18, 4.25, 4.32, 5.21  and 5.30 of the Report. The Committee 
has accepted the explanations furnished by the Ministry and does not wish to pursue 
those further as of now, under chapter II of the Report. 
5. The recommendations/observations in respect of which Committee has not 
accepted replies given by the Ministry. T hose are under  paras 2.53, 2.42, 3.13, 3.15, 
3.22, 3.26, 3.29, 3.35, 3.45, 3.50, 3.54, 4.10, 4.12, 4.14, 4.24, 4.36, 5.3, 5.6, 5.14 and 
5.28 of the Report. The Committee expresses its concern over non -acceptance of it s 
recommendations.  Those are dealt under Chapter – III of this Report and reiterates its 
recommendations.  
6. The recommendations/observations on which final replies of the Ministry of Law 
and Justice have not been received  relate to paras 2.19, 2.23 and 4.20 of the Report. 
The Committee asked the Ministry to furnish the final replies to these paras at the 
earliest, under Chapter IV of the Report. 
  

2 
 
CHAPTER - I 
RECOMMENDATIONS / OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN 
ACCEPTED BY THE MINISTRY 
DEPARTMENT OF LEGAL AFFAIRS 
Recommendation/Observation of the Committee 
1. It was also pointed out that notaries appointed under central quota are not 
evenly distributed in the State. Some of the districts are over - represented while some 
of the districts are under -represented. The Committee, therefore, desires that while 
making appointment, focus should be given to appoint notaries in those districts of the 
State, which are under-represented or not represented.                               (Para 4.11) 
Action Taken / proposed to be taken by the Department 
1.1 The Notary Cell of t his Department is appointing Notaries for taluka, district 
level in each of the State, however the Notary Cell is deeply examining the issue of 
even distribution of central quotas of notaries in respective State/UT. In the 
forthcoming exercise for holding interviews for selection of notaries in various 
States/UTs, it will be ensured that notaries are appointed in under-represented districts 
which have fairly less number of notaries. The applications will be scrutinized 
minutely to ensure that under - represented districts will also have sufficient strength 
of notaries public, so that public will not have to travel towards cities/districts for 
notary work.  
Committee’s further observation 
1.2 The Committee notes the reply of the Department . The Committee feels  
that under representation of notaries in certain Talukas/ Districts affects the 
justice delivery process at grassroots level and desires to be apprised of the 
outcomes of actions/ initiatives undertaken to appoint notaries from under 
represented Districts and States in its Action Taken Notes.  
Recommendation/Observation of the Committee 
1.3 The Committee, therefore, desires that while making appointment due 
consideration should be given to inclusiveness of the notaries and desires that the 
Department should furnish the data of social category of notaries to the Committee 
while submitting its Action Taken Replies.                                     (Para 4.13) 
Action Taken/proposed to be taken by the Department 
1.4 In terms of Rule 3 of the Notaries Rules, 1956, persons who had been 
practicing for at least ten years are eligible for appointment as notary. Persons 
belonging to Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes and other backward classes who had 
been practicing for at least seven years are eligible for appointment as notary. Further, 
women who had been practicing for at least seven years are also eligible for 
appointment as notary.  In the selection process for notaries, members of the interview 
boards give due weightage to each of the above noted categories. B esides these, 

3 
 
reasonable due representation are also given to senior citizens, physically challenged 
persons. 
1.5   In the year 2018 -19, a total number of 8960 notaries were appointed by the 
Central Government, which included 963 belonging to Scheduled Caste, 76 belonging 
to Scheduled Tribes and 3530 belonging to OBC category. 
Committee’s further observation  
1.6 The Committee is pleased to note that the Department is following policies of 
positive discrimination while considering appointment of notaries.  
DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE 
Recommendation/Observation of the Committee 
1.7 The Committee observes that both act ual requirements and expenses of 
National Judicial Academy (NJA) are more than allocations for the last few years. 
The Committee notes that the NJA is a premier institution of the country for the 
training of judges of Higher Judiciary, judges of neighborin g countries, /District 
Courts and Tribunals, etc. and plays an important role in leveraging soft power of the 
country in the field of judicial training and research. The Committee, accordingly, 
recommends the Department to approach Ministry of Finance for enhanced 
allocations to NJA as approved by it at RE stage during the Financial Year 2020 -21, 
so that on -going training and research activities of the Academy are not hampered 
due to financial constraints. The action taken on the recommendations of the 
Committee may be apprised by the Department in its Action Taken Replies.  
                                                             (Para 2.36) 
Action Taken / proposed to be taken by the Department 
 
1.8 The observations of the Committee have been noted and necessary action will 
be taken at the time of formulation of Budget proposals at RE stage for the coming 
Financial Year 2020-21. 
 
Committee’s further observation 
 
1.9 The Committee notes the reply of the Department. 
Recommendation/Observation of the Committee 
1.10 The Committee notes that there is no under utilization in the current Financial 
Year. The Committee is also of the view that National Legal Services Authority 
(NALSA) needs to rationalise its expenses relati ng to Legal Counsel Fee by engaging 
more and more Senior Lawyers on pro-bono basis. Further, expenses relating to Mass 
Awareness Programme needs to be rationalized to eliminate wasteful expenditure, if 
any.                                                                                               (Para 2.39) 
 Action Taken / proposed to be taken by the Department 
 
1.11 DRSC has observed that NALSA may engage more and more senior lawyers 

4 
 
on pro-bono basis.  It is submitted that various SLSAs are requesting  senior lawyers 
to take up cases on pro -bono basis and are successful in many cases. NALSA shall 
further advise all the SLSAs to make efforts to involve more and more senior lawyers 
on pro-bono basis, so as to reduce the financial burden in making payment to 30,000 
panel lawyers having practice of more than 10 years who are being paid as per the 
declared fee schedule. 
 
1.12 Regarding Legal Awareness program, it is submitted that from April 2019 to 
February 2020, 2.13 lacs awareness programmes were held thro ughout the country by 
various SLSAs/DLSAs which were attended by 2.91 crore persons. NALSA will be 
taking steps towards promoting use of technology for such legal literacy programmes 
so that similar number of people may be covered with lesser expenses. This will result 
in the reduction of expenses to some extent. 
 
Committee’s further observation 
 
1.13 The Committee has noted the reply of the Department and recommends 
that social networking websites which are economical and accessible to many 
should be utilized for legal awareness campaigns.   
Vacancies in Courts  
Recommendation/Observation of the Committee 
1.14 A judgment delivered by a Division Bench of the Supreme Court on 17 th 
February, 2020 in the case M/s PLR Projects Pvt. Ltd. vs. Mahanadi Coalfields 
Limited & others has been brought to the notice of the Committee. The apex court has 
observed that the High Courts must make endeavours to recommend the names 
against the vacancies as early as possible and High Courts should keep on 
recommending names without waiting for the result of the earlier recommendations 
till all recommendations are made.  The C ommittee appreciates the aforesaid 
judgement of the Apex Court and expect that concerned High Courts should 
recommend the names well in advance so that the appointees to the post of judges in 
the High Courts are available on the very date of the retirement of the judges.  
                                                                                                 (Para 3.14) 
Action Taken / proposed to be taken by the Department 
1.15 The Hon’ble  Supreme Court vide Order dated 17.02.2020 requested the 
Registrars General of different High Courts to file their responses regarding vacant 
position, date of their occurrence, number of vacancies likely to arise in next six 
months and the time period for  making recommendation for filling up vacancies with 
4 weeks to hear the case again on 23.3.2020.However, the matter could not be heard 
on 23.3.2020 in view of COVID-19 pandemic. 
Committee’s further observation 
 
1.16 The Committee has noted the reply of th e Ministry and would like to be 
apprised of the further development in the matter. 

5 
 
Recommendation/Observation of the Committee 
1.17 The Committee is concerned with the large number of vacancies of Judicial 
Officers in Subordinate Judiciary. As per the data  made available to the Committee, 
as on 20 th February, 2020, around 21 percent of sanctioned strength (24,018) of 
Judicial Officers in Subordinate Courts is vacant in different States. Out of 5,146 
vacancies a large number of vacancies are in the States of  Uttar Pradesh (1,053), 
Bihar (776), Madhya Pradesh (370), Gujarat (308) and Rajasthan (309). Despite, the 
Supreme Court monitoring vacancy positions of Judicial Officers in Subordinate 
judiciary through hearings on Malik Mazhar Sultan and Anr vs. UP Publi c Service 
Commission (2007) case, a large number of vacancies of Judicial Officers are 
existing in various States.  The Committee, therefore, recommends the Department of 
Justice to impress upon the State Governments/High Courts to expedite the process of 
filling up of the vacancy positions of Judicial Officers in Subordinate Courts as per 
the directions of the Supreme Court in the Malik Mazhar Sultan and Anr vs. UP 
Public Service Commission (2007) case.                (Para 3.18) 
Action Taken / proposed to be taken by the Department 
 
1.18 The Government has been taking up the issue of filling up of vacancies in 
District and Subordinate Courts with the respective High Courts and State 
Governments. A  series of meetings were held with Registrars General of all High 
Courts and Law Secretaries of all State Governments / UTs through Video 
Conferencing in the month of January, 2018, July, 2018 and November, 2018 and 
September-October, 2019 to follow up on filling up posts of Judicial Officers in 
District and Sub ordinate Courts.  The Department of Justice has hosted a web -portal 
on its website for reporting and monitoring of sanctioned and working strength, and 
vacancies of Judicial Officers of District and Subordinate Courts on monthly basis. 
 
As on Sanctioned Strength Working Strength Vacancies 
31.12.2013 19,518 15,115 4403 
31.03.2020 24,037 19,167 4870 
  
1.19 To ensure that the vacancies at the District and Subordinate Courts level are 
filled up on time, High Courts in consultation with the State Governments are 
required to adhere to the time frame prescribed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the 
case of Malik Ma zhar Sultan and Anr Vs U.P. Public Service Commission  [Civil 
Appeal No. 1867 of 2006 decided on January 4, 2007]. The process for recruitment of 
judges in subordinate courts should commence on 31st March of a calendar year and 
end by 31st October of the sa me year. State Governments and High Courts have been 
again requested on 30.04.2020 to expedite filling of vacancies in District and 
Subordinate Courts as per guidelines of the Supreme Court which is also being 
monitored by Supreme Court in Malik Mazhar Sultan case.

Paperless Election for Local Bodies 
 
Recommendation/Observation of the Committee 
 
2.34    The ECI has also unequivocally been reiterating that EVMs are tamper proof 
and integrity of electoral process is well preserved with its use accompanied with 
VVPATs in the participatory democracy.  Booth capturing and casting of invalid votes 
have become the thingof the pastwith the aforesaid digital revolution. In this regard, 
the Committee points out that in  most of  the  States,  election  to  Panchayati  Raj  
Institutions  and  Municipal Bodies are still being  held  thro ugh  ballot  papers.  The 
advancement of technology in election process needs to percolate to local bodies.  
The Committee is of the view that election to local bodies should also be held through 
Electronic Voting Machine accompanied by VVPAT. The Committe e, therefore, 
recommends the Election Commission of India to impress upon the State Election 
Commissions for use of EVMs and VVPATs available with ECI for paperless election 
to local bodies for ease of the electors.                                                      (Para 5.21) 
 
Action Taken / proposed to be taken by the Department 
 
2.35 In  respect  of   the recommendation of the Parliamentary Standing 
Committee regarding impressing upon the State Election Commissions for use of 
EVMs and VVPATs by the Election Commission of India, it is pertinent  to  mention  
that  the  Election  Commission   of   India   is  entrusted for conduct of elections to 
the  Office  of  the  Hon’ble  President  of  India, Office of the  Hon’b1e Vice -
President of India,  the  House of the  People and  the State Legislature. Elections to 
the House of  the  People  and  State Legislative  Assemblies  are  only  being  
conducted  using   EVMs  and VVPATs. 
 
2.36 Further, the conduct of elections to the Panchayats and Municipal bodies are 
entrusted with the State Election Commissions, which are independent bodies and 
have their own laws and procedures for conducting such elections. 
 

20 
 
2.37 It is also mentioned here that EVMs being used by the Election Commission 
of India can be used only for single post elections. However, elections to the local 
bodies are generally multi -post elections.  Some SECs use EVMs in their elections 
and have their own protocols so far as the storage, security, transportation and usage 
of EVMs. However, State Election Commissions had been provided ECI -EVMs by 
the ECI, whenever, they made request to loan ECI -EVMs for conducting the lo cal 
body/ Panchayat elections. The ECI has no authority over the SECs  and hence, has 
no say in their  handling  or  usage  of  EVMs  but  has  always been looked upon for 
answers in case of any allegation on  the  EVM operation / functioning, Since EVMs 
belonged to ECI and were of the same type. Of late this has become very frequent. 
Also,  the  loaning  process entails several costs and responsibilities like inventory 
management, warehousing at both ends,  and  transportation  cost  for  to  and  fro 
movement of machines. Above all, in the present  day  highly  charged political 
atmosphere, it would be extremely difficult to  defend  any aspersions on EVMs 
which are  neither  in  ECI’s  control  nor  handled  by the people over whom the 
Commission has auth ority. Hence, the Commission has decided to stop loaning and 
instead transfer the ownership of the M2 EVMs and VVPATs to the SECs and to 
sever all tieswith these machines so that the onus of answering questions on the 
performance and integrity of the SEC m achines lies squarely on the respective SEC. 
The Commission has decided that it will not be using M2 EVMs and M2 VVPATs 
and will be using M3 EVMs and M3 VVPATs only and these will not be allowed to 
be supplied to any other organization by the manufacturers. 
 
2.38 In the constant endeavor to conduct the local body elections through electronic 
means and to ensure the transparency of voting through use of VVPATs is 
maintained, the ECI  had  already  requested  the  Ministry  of Law and Justice to 
grant No Obj ection Certificate for the transfer of ownership of 5,57,000 BUs, 
5,30,000 CUs of M-2 make and 2,71,000 VVPATs of M -2 make to the State Election  
Commissions  at  a  nominal price of Rs. 1/ - per BU, CU and VVPAT each. The M-2 
make VVPATs are compatible with the CUs and BUs of M-2 make EVMs only. 
 
2.39 It is further stated that the proposed transfer is a Government to Government 
transfer and no private party is involved. The transferred machines will be used for 
conducting elections only so that people’s ma ndate is judged in a 'free and fair 
manner.  All the States do not have the same purchasing power so only the capital 
cost of the machines will be borne by Government of India and the States will be 
responsible for the transportation, storage, security and  repairs of the machines. 
Further, as per the prevalent practice, the States buy the consumables like paper roll, 
power packs, security seals etc whenever they conduct local body elections. 
 
2.40 Hence, the transfer of ownership of the M -2 EVMs and VVPATs to the State 
Electoral Commissions, at a nominal price of Rs. 1/ - per BU, CU and VVPAT each 
may be done to ensure the conduct of free fair and transparent election, provided 
NOC is granted to the Commission by the Ministry of Law and Justice.

Recommendation/Observation of the Committee 
3. The Committee appreciates the initiatives of Department of Legal Affairs to

application for not ary-ship certificate due to infrastructural constraints. Instances of

come to the notice of the Committee. The Committee, therefore, desires that the 
infrastructural capacity of  the Department may be overhauled for streamlining 
issuance and renewal of certificate of notary. The applicant should be given an 
opportunity to track his/her application and there should be a moratorium period for 
the applications received after which th e applicants may be required to file fresh 
applications.                      (Para 4.10) 
Action Taken / proposed to be taken by the Department 
3.1 The Notary Cell of this Department receives Online Applications for 
appointments of Notaries for all of States/UTs. Vide Notaries (Third Amendment 
Rules) 2019 published in GSR 821(E) dated 05.11.2019, the Rule 8B of the Notary 
Rules 1956 has been amended a nd procedure for renewal for Practice of Certificate 
has been amended and an application for Certificate of Practice shall be submitted 
online in Form XVI to the appropriate Government before (six months) from the date 
of expiry of its period of validity.

inviting renewal certificates of notaries six months before its expiry, however, the

should be operationalised to enable candidates to check status of their online 

23 
 
applications. The Committee also feels that the Department should process the

Seeding of Aadhar with Electors’ Photo Identity Card (EPIC)  
Recommendation/Observation of the Committee 
3.72   The Committee understands that free and fair elections are the bedrock 
of democracy and the latter is a Basic Feature of the Constitution. An error -
free   Electoral   Roll   is   sine qua non of free and fair election. The 
Committee has been advocat ing linkage of unique Aadhaar ID card number 
with Voter I-card which would streamline alterations in EPIC during change 
of ordinary residence by the electors. The incidence of multiple entry could 
also be eliminated which is required in participative democ racy. The 
committee, therefore, recommends that the Government may undertake 
appropriate actions for the purpose of linking unique Aadhaar Card number 
with Voter ID card to purify the electoral roll, which is in larger interest of 
democratic policy.                                                                              (Para 5.14) 
Action Taken / proposed to be taken by the Department 
3.73     The Commission has already sent its proposals on linking of Aadhar 
Card Number with the voter Id to purify ele ctoral to the Ministry of Law and 
justice vide its letter No. 3/ER/2018/SDR dated 13 th August, 2019. Extract of 
the proposals sent to the M/o Law and Justice vide its letter dated 22/11/1999 
is as under. 
“In order to leverage the availability of unique ide ntification 
number by way of Aadhaar numbers for purifying the electoral 
rolls, the Commission had, in 2015, started collecting the 
Aadhaar Numbers of electors who volunteered to provide the 
same. However, the programme had to be suspended in view of 
the directions in the Interim Order dated 11 thAugust, 2015, of the 
Hon’ble Supreme Court in WP(C) No. 494 of 2012 (Justice K S 
Puttuswamy’s case), prohibiting using of information about 
Aadhaar details for any purpose other than the PDS Scheme and 
LPG Distribution Scheme. 
Hon’ble Supreme Court has since passed its final judgment in the 
matters relating to Aadhaar issue. The Commission has 
considered the matter further in view of the directions in the 
Judgment.  The Commission is keen to make use of the unique ID  
numbers provided by Aadhaar Scheme for cleaning the electoral 
rolls. An error free electoral roll forms the basis for a credible 
election. Therefore, it would be in national interest to use 
the Aadhaar  Numbers for verification purposes to ensure 
the identity of applicants and to prevent multiple enrolment 
of same person in the electoral roll. In view of the above  
quoted  observations   made by the Hon’ble Supreme Court 
it is not possible to link Aadhaa r with EPIC (Voter ID) 
without bringing appropriate statutory amendments.  
Accordingly, the Commission proposed  the  appropriate  

39 
 
amendments  may be made in the Representation of the  
People  Act,  1950 and  in the Aadhaar  Act  for permitting the 
election machinery  to  obtain  and  use  the  Aadhaar  
Numbers for the purposes of electoral roll as  a  back -end  
exercise.  It is, further, clarified  that the Aadhaar Numbers

One Nation One Electoral Roll 
Recommendation/Observation of the Committee 
3.76     The  Committee  observes  that  there  is  a  lot  of commonalities 
between the  elections   to   Lok   Sabha and  State Legislative Assemblies on 
the one hand and that of  to local  bodies  on  the  other.  The eligibility 
criterion of the elector for all  three aforesaid elections is the same. It is the 
same individual who is called upon by two different Constitutional authorities 
to cast his/ hour vote at different point of time for different bodies in the same 
territorial constituencies in which his/her names is registered in the Electoral 
Roll. Furthermore, the First- Past- the -Post system is followed to declare the 
winner in all three elections.  Even the wordings used about Electoral Roll in 
Articles 324 and 243(K) and 243 Z (A) of the Constitution ar e identical.  The 
Committee has been recommending   time and   again in its 88 th, 91st and 96th 
Reports for Common Electoral Roll from local body to Lok Sabha Elections. It 
would not only save time, energy and resources of concerned State 
Government but al so obviate confusion in the mind of voters. The data of 
electors available in National Voters Service Portal (NVSP) maintained by 
the Election Commission of India could be readily used by the State Election 
Commissions without hassle. Electronic Voting Mac hine  and  VVPAT  which 
are available with the Election Commission  of  India  can  also  be  utilized  
by  the State  Election Commission   for  election  to  local  bodies   having   
Common Electoral Roll. The Committee, therefore, again recommends for 
common electoral roll for local body to Lok Sabha Election.                                                                                                       
                                                                 (Para 5.28)
   
  

40 
 
Action Taken / proposed to be taken by the Department 
3.77     The Commission has already sent its proposal on use of Common 
Electoral Rolls at elections conducted by the Election Commission and the 
State Election Commissions vide letter dated 22/11/1999 and subsequentl y 
reiterated in several times. It was reiterated vide the Hon’b1e CEC’s D.O 
letter dated 26 th July 2019. Extract of the proposals sent  to  the  M/o  Law  
and Justice vide its letter dated 22/11/1999 is as under. 
 
“Use of Common Electoral Rolls at elections conducted by the 
Election Commission and the State Election Commissions"  
(Proposal made in Chief Election Commissioner's letter dated 22nd 
November, 1999 addressed to the Prime Minister)  
Superintendence, direct ion and control of the preparation and 
revision of electoral rolls for elections to the House of the People and 
the State Legislative Assemblies is the function entrusted to the 
Election Commission by Article 324(1) of the Constitution. Likewise, 
superintendence, direction and control of the preparation and revision 
of electoral rolls for elections to the Local Bodies has been entrusted 
to the State Election Commissioners by Articles 243K and 243ZA of 
the Constitution, as inserted by the Constitution (73rd and 74th 
Amendments) Acts, 1992. The preparation and revision of electoral 
rolls for Parliamentary and Assembly Constituencies are governed by 
the  provisions of the R.P. Act, 1950 made by Parliament, whereas,  
the preparation  and revision  of rolls for l ocal bodies elections are 
regulated by the State laws of the State concerned. Most of the State 
laws provide that the electoral rolls prepared by the Election 
Commission for Parliamentary and Assembly elections should be the 
basis for the preparation and r evision of rolls for local bodies 
elections. Whereas, in some of the States,  it is further  provided  that  
the Parliamentary and Assembly rolls will be adopted in toto for local 
bodies elections, in other States, the Parliamentary and Assembly 
Rolls are to be  adopted  only as  the draft rolls for local body 
elections and they are subjected  to  further modifications by way of 
inclusions and deletions. In some of the cases, even the qualifying 
dates for the Parliamentary/Assembly rolls and local body roll s are 
different. This not only creates confusion among the electors because 
their names may be present in one roll but absent in the other, or vice 
versa, but also results in duplication of effort and expenditure. In 
almost all the eases, the same machiner y at the field level is entrusted 
the job of preparing and revising rolls for both types of elections. The 
electoral rolls for Parliamentary and Assembly Constituencies are 
prepared, and revised under the strict superintendence, direction and 
control of the Election Commission, with due care and caution and by 
incurring considerable expenditure. It will be a huge national saving, 
if there are common rolls for all elections, and  the Parliamentary and 
Assembly rolls are used for local bodies elections also, by being 

41 
 
adopted and rearranged, by the method of ‘Cut and Paste'  according  
to the wards or polling areas of the local bodies. This will not pose 
any problems to the electoral machinery in the field as it is the same 
at the ground level. This may need so me minor amendments to the 
local laws of the States concerned, but will sub -serve great national 
interest of economy in government expenditure on elections. It may be 
important to note that in order to reduce such expenditure, many of 
the common items of p olling materials like, ballot boxes, are already 
being used for all elections to Parliament, State Legislatures and 
Local Bodies.” 
3.78 Further, in 2004, in Consolidated Proposals for Electoral Reforms, the 
Election Commission had proposed that there shoul d be common rolls for all 
elections, with the Parliamentary and Assembly rolls adapted to suit the needs 
of local bodies’ elections. This is primarily recommended by the Commission 
for the purpose of saving or expenditure and administrative effort and to m ake 
the process more efficient. 
3.79 Election Commission of India has  issued  instructions  to  the  Chief 
Electoral Officers of all the States /UTs vide its letter dated 10th December, 
2008 to share the computerized electoral database with the Stat Elect ion 
Commissions so that they could  generate  electoral  rolls according  to the  
extent  of their panchayat/local body wards from the same database. The terms 
and conditions for sharing of electoral roll database have also been specified. 
3.80 It is also stated that the common electoral roll for local bodies and Lok 
Sabha elections may need amendments to the relevant provision of 
Registration of Electors Rule 1960 and The Representation of the People’s 
Act, 1950. 
3.81 The proposa1 is yet to be approved. 
 
Committee’s further observation 
3.82 The Committee observes that the proposal for common Electoral Roll in 
the country was initiated by the Commission nearly 20 years back, however, it is 
yet to be materialized. The Committee is in agreement with the views of the 
Commission that creation of common Electoral Roll in the country from 
Panchayat to Parliament will  save unnecessary expenditure and reduce 
administrative works of various electoral agencies and at the same 
time making the electoral process more effi cient. The Committee, 
accordingly, feels that Commission and the Ministry of Law and 
Justice may examine and prepare a brief note on the issue of Common 
Electoral Roll, along with the reasons for not taking up the issue 
despite reiteration by the Election Commission in the year 2019 and 
apprise the same to the Committee.

3.83 The Committee is apprised that the Institute of Legislative Drafting and

observes that there is real dearth of good quality draftsmen in the Country. The 
Committee desires that drafting errors and ambiguity in the law may be avoided by 
making effective pre-legislative consultation with stakeholders. For that purpose, the 
Bills should be available in regional languages for wider consultation with 
stakeholders. The Committee also desires that Acts allocated to the Department under 
the Allocation of Business Rules, 1961 may be periodically reviewed on the basis of 
its use as part of post legislative scrutiny. The loopholes and infirmities pointed to the 
Department by the stakeholders of the law may be submitted to the Committee in its 
action taken replies.                                                                                       (Para. 5.3) 
Action Taken / proposed to be taken by the Department 
3.84 It is submit ted that so far as making availability of Bills in Regional 
Languages is concerned it is submitted that the regional language Unit is responsible 
for preparation of the regional text of the Central Acts only. If desired the Bills in 
Regional languages may also be prepared, if proper setup or infrastructure like Hindi 
Branch of O.L. Wing is made available or provided. 
 
Committee’s further observation 
3.85 The Committee notes the reply of the Department on the issue of 
availability of Bills in regional langua ges. The Committee also notes that the 
Department has not furnished its replies with respect to the post legislative 
scrutiny of Acts and accordingly, desires that replies pertaining to post legislative 
scrutiny of Acts may be furnished to it in the Action  Taken Notes of the 
Department. 
Recommendation/Observation of the Committee 
3.86 The Committee in its Ninety-sixth report on the Demands for Grants (2018-19) 
has recommended for bringing out authoritative text of the Constitution of India and 
other Central  Acts in all the language mentioned under the Eighth Schedule of the 
Constitution. The Committee observes that the Department has not been able to bring 
authoritative text of the Constitution of India and other Central Acts in all Scheduled 
languages of th e Constitution. The Committee, accordingly, recommends to the 
Department to expedite the translation works of Constitution/Acts/Subordinate 
Legislations in remaining scheduled languages.                                             (Para 5.6) 
Action Taken / proposed to be taken by the Department 
 
3.87  This wing is making all efforts to publish the Constitution of India in all the 
languages as enshrined in the Eighth schedule of the constitution of India and so far 
have succeeded to publish in sixteen regional languages and it is available on the 
official website on the Ministry . The Constitution of India in Dogri and Kashmiri 
Languages is at advance stage and efforts are being made to publish the same shortly. 

43 
 
The sixth and updated edition of the Constitution of India in Urdu, Eighth Edition of 
Marathi, third edition of Tamil and second edition of Punjabi is under progress. 
 
3.88 Due to non -availability of sufficient infrastructure and sufficient staff in the 
official languages wing of the Ministry of Law and Justice , the Official Languages 
Wing of the L egislative Department in the Ministry of Law and Justice in close 
collaboration and co-operation with the respective State Government has been getting 
the Central Acts translated in eleven regional languages by the concerned State 
Governments. Therefore, k eeping in view of the importance of Central Acts in the 
day-to-day functioning in courts, local authorities and Tribunals etc, as well as social 
importance in day -to-day life, the priority lists of Central Acts are prepared by this 
Department periodically and sent to the State Governments concerned for preparing 
their regional versions. The progress made so far in the preparation and publication of 
Central Acts in the said eleven languages is shown at (Annexure-VIII). As on date, 
regional version of 1160 Ce ntral Acts in different languages is available on the 
official website of the Department . However, Regional language Unit is expediting 
and progressing to publish the updated version of the Constitution of India and 
Authoritative Texts of the Central Acts in all the Scheduled languages enshrined in 
the Constitution of India. 
 
Committee’s further observation 
3.89 The Committee notes the replies of the Department. As on date, the 
Constitution of India has been published in only sixteen Scheduled languages 
and out of that no updated edition of Constitution of India has been brought in 
Telugu, Odia, Bengali since 1980, 1981, and 1987, respectively. Further, out of 
the 22 Scheduled languages of the Constitution, the Committee observes that the 
preamble to the Constitution is not available in Bodo, Dogri, Kashmiri, and 
Santhali on its website. With regard to preparation, publication and uploading of 
Central Acts in Scheduled languages, it has been observed that it is being 
undertaken in only 11 Scheduled languages. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends the Department to expedite updation, translation of Constitution of 
India and authoritative texts of Central Acts in all the languages contained in the 
Eighth Schedule of the Constitution.  
3.90 The Committee also observes that large numbers of posts of draftspersons 
are vacant in the Department, Official Languages Wing and Vidhi Sahitya 
Prakashan. Out of 44 sanctioned positions, 9 are vacant in the Department, out 
of 151 sanctioned positions, 56 are vacant in the Official Languages Wing, and 
out of 75 sanctioned positions, 24 are vacant in the Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan. The 
Committee feels that with the ever-increasing number of drafting of legislations 
year after year, the existing human resources of the Department needs optimally 
utilized and, if required, to be augmented for quality drafting. The Committee 
also feels that existing vacancy positions are directly related to the non-
availability of texts/ Acts in Scheduled languages and quality of drafting of 
legislations, and therefore, the Committee desires that actions undertaken by the 
Department in this year to fill up the vacancy positions may be furnished to it in 
the Action Taken Notes of the Department.

 I, the Chairman of the Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee

Committee to submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this One Hundred 
sixth Report on Demands for Grants (20 21-22) pertaining to the Ministry of 
Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions. 
2. In accordance with the constitutional requirement under Article 113, the 
estimated expenditure of Ministries/Departments of Government of India project ed 
under various Demands for Grants for the upcoming financial year need s to be voted 
by Parliament. As a sequel thereto, Demands for Grants of the relevant 
Ministries/Departments stand referred to the concerned Department -related 
Parliamentary Standing Committee to make a close scrutiny thereof under Rule 270 of 
Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Council of States. While making 
scrutiny of Demands for Grants the Committee has made an appraisal of performance, 
programmes, policies of the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievance s and Pension s 
vis-à-vis expenditure made out of Consolidated Fund of India in the current financial 
year. 
3. In this Report, a scrutiny of Demand Nos. 73, 7 4 and 83 pertaining to  the 
Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances & Pensions, Central Vigilance Commission 
(CVC) and Union P ublic Service Commission (UPSC), respectively , for the financial 
year 2021-22 has been made by the Committee.

R E P O R T 
CHAPTER – I 
OVERVIEW OF THE MINISTRY 
Introduction 
1.0. The Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions is the nodal Ministry for 
personnel management in the Government of India. It formulates policies with respect to 
recruitment, training, career progression, staff welfare, post retirement dispensation 
administrative reforms, vigilance administration, grievance redressal, good governance and 
pensioners’ welfare.  
1.1. The Ministry comprises the following three Departments: 
(i) Department of Personnel and Training (DoP&T) 
(ii) Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances  
            (DARPG) 
(iii) Department of Pension and Pensioners' Welfare (DPPW) 
 
 
1.2. The Ministry is presently under the overall charge of the Hon’ble Prime Minister 
assisted by the Minister of State. The Department of Personnel and Training is functioning 
under the charge of a Secretary while the Department of Administrative Reforms & Public 
Grievances and the Department of Pensions and Pensioners’ Welfare are functioning under the 
charge of another Secretary. 
Evolution of the Ministry 
1.3. In March, 1954, an Organisation and Method (O&M) Division was set up in the 
Cabinet Secretariat to oversee the work relating to Administrative Reforms. Subsequently, in 
March, 1964, a Department of Administrative Reforms was set up within the Ministry of 
Home Affairs and Organisation and Method (O & M) Division was transferred to its charge 
from the Cabinet Secretariat. On 7th February, 1973, the work relating to Department of 
Administrative Reforms was transferred to Department of Personnel created under Cabinet 
Secretariat on 01st August, 1970 and was re-designated as Department of Personnel and
